newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia on edge as confident Yeltsin has operation.
newsitem.headline: Russia on edge as confident Yeltsin has operation.

text.p: A confident Boris Yeltsin went into the operating theatre at dawn on Tuesday for a heart bypass operation that aims to restore the president to the Kremlin after months in which Russia has looked dangerously leaderless.
"Are you here with the knife already?" the 65-year-old leader jokingly asked his doctors, his spokesman said.

His final act before going under the anaesthetic at 7 a.m. (0400 GMT) was to hand over power, including Russia's nuclear trigger, to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, one of several figures manoeuvring for position around the sick president.
Yeltsin will take back control once he comes round from the surgery. He issued a written statement saying he was confident of recovery and reassuring Russians there was no power vacuum.

"Not for a minute will the country be without a leader with full powers," Yeltsin said. "He (Chernomyrdin) and my other colleagues are tested and reliable people. They will have big responsibility in the time to come."
"I am sure everything will go alright," he added. "I believe I will soon be working at full strength, as I did before."
Chernomyrdin, 58, and a possible successor, has effectively been running the country since Yeltsin's reelection on July 3.

As Yeltsin went under the surgeon's knife, thousands marched in Russia's Far East in strikes and demonstrations called by trade unions to protest against unpaid wages -- the most potent symbol of the country's massive economic problems.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who faces reelection on Tuesday, sent Yeltsin "best wishes for a speedy recovery". The Russian Orthodox Church has called for prayers.
Western leaders see Yeltsin, who led Russia out of communism in 1991, as the guarantor of Russia's shaky democracy and fear his loss could plunge it into a period of deeper instability.
"The president is the main stabilising factor in the country," Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, another potential presidential hopeful, commented to Interfax news agency.
Bypass surgery improves blood supply to the heart by grafting in veins to divert blood around blockages -- in Yeltsin's case three or four -- in the cardiac arteries.

It was being performed by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin, 50, who previously performed a bypass on Chernomyrdin. Michael DeBakey, the 88-year-old U.S. cardiologist who pioneered the bypass technique more than 30 years ago, was advising him.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said three Russian surgeons were assisting Akchurin. No foreigners were present at first but DeBakey was due in the theatre during the morning. The operation was likely to last six to eight hours, he said.
Hundreds of bypass operations are performed around the world every day. Only some two percent fail.
Medical experts say the biggest risk to the president may be problems with other organs, like his liver. Two German doctors specialised in post-operative complications are on hand.
Yeltsin's motorcade swept into the Cardiology Research Centre in suburban Moscow before dawn. The president had been prepared for surgery at the Barvikha state sanatorium nearby.
He announced the operation on television in a moment of unprecedented candour on September 5.
That ended weeks of equivocation by aides who had been explaining Yeltsin's absence since before his reelection by saying he had a cold and various other minor ailments.
The admission that the president, who had two heart attacks last year, needed major surgery also fueled a bitter struggle for influence in the Kremlin.
It involved notably Chernomyrdin, chief of the presidential staff Anatoly Chubais and General Alexander Lebed, a political maverick roped in to the Kremlin to secure victory at the polls.

Yeltsin finally sacked Lebed on October 17 amid a flurry of accusations and counter-accusations of mysterious plots and plans to seize power. Lebed has warned of an army mutiny over unpaid wages, but few analysts see a military bid for power.

The 46-year-old former paratrooper, his popularity assured by his success in ending the deeply unpopular Chechen war, remains a key political figure. Polls show he would be a strong contender for the presidency if Yeltsin had to step down.
If that were to happen Chernomyrdin would rule in the interim with a mandate to hold an election within three months.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, would also be a challenger in a new vote. He complained the Kremlin cheated to beat him in July by concealing that Yeltsin had a third heart attack days before the second-round vote.
